6: ULYÁNA. What are you saying? Married a beggar and you're putting on airs. Do you think that you've married the daughter of a distinguished landowner? KRASNÓV. What I think—is my business, and you can't understand it with your wits. You'd better keep still.
5: ULYÁNA. Why are you giving yourself such airs all of a sudden, sister? Am I worse than you? You just wait awhile, you'll taste all that. We can clip your wings, too. KRASNÓV. Yes, but be careful.
4: KÚRITSYN. Ah, brother! Beat your overcoat and it will be warmer; beat a wife—she'll be smarter. TATYÁNA. Not every wife will allow herself to be beaten, and the one that allows it, isn't worth any other treatment.
3: ULYÁNA. Yes, that's so, that used to happen. I can say that without shame, to everybody. KRASNÓV. There's nothing good in that, just swagger.
2: TATYÁNA. Every one to his own taste! You, sister, like such treatment, while I consider it the height of rudeness. LUKÉRYA. Nowadays, such peasant's conduct is discarded everywhere; it's getting out of fashion.
0: ULYÁNA. [ With a start ] I just said that for instance, Manuylo Kalinich. Because, sister, women like us can't live without strict discipline. It's a true proverb: "If you beat your wife, the soup tastes better."
